testedDecision: Classify which admission and Stage 1 findings are genuine cues of impaired superior vena cava venous return versus spared or nonspecific findings.
reason: The keyed set follows from baseline and Stage 1 upper-body congestion, but the sluggish right forearm IV is the one segment that still needs real inference. Stage 2 removes that inference by reporting that the same forearm IV infiltrated and that both upper extremities developed pitting edema. That exposure settles the venous-obstruction reading of an otherwise ambiguous Stage 1 cue.

testedDecision: Select superior vena cava syndrome from extrinsic mediastinal compression as the condition explaining the Stage 1 upper-body congestion cue cluster.
reason: Stage 3 records that interventional radiology was consulted for possible SVC stenting and that dexamethasone was started, naming the keyed diagnosis and its mechanism outright. Stage 2 adds bilateral upper-extremity pitting edema and a rising neck circumference, which further eliminates the isolated arm clot and heart failure distractors. A learner reading the exposed record never has to reason from the Stage 1 cue cluster.

testedDecision: Choose new inspiratory stridor as the most immediately life-threatening Stage 2 change among tachycardia, rising neck circumference, and falling oxygen saturation.
reason: Stage 3 reports that stridor is no longer audible over the trachea as the headline result of escalation, singling stridor out from the other Stage 2 changes as the tracked emergency. The same stage shows neck circumference and oxygen requirement still abnormal, which demotes those competing options. The priority ranking the part asks for is therefore already performed in the exposed record.

testedDecision: Select the immediate Stage 2 nursing actions for new stridor: raise oxygen, keep the bed elevated, escalate to the provider, stage airway equipment.
reason: Stage 3 narrates the keyed actions as accomplished facts: the nurse escalated to the provider, oxygen was raised to high-flow nasal cannula, and the head of bed stayed elevated. It also shows the replacement line going to a lower extremity, which discredits the distractor of attempting a left forearm IV before calling for help. Three of the four keyed selections can simply be read off the exposed stage.

testedDecision: Choose non-upper-extremity peripheral access coordinated with policy and the team, rather than another arm site, given obstructed superior vena cava drainage.
reason: Stage 3 states that a new peripheral IV was placed in the left lower extremity after coordination with the team and per facility policy, restating the keyed option almost word for word. That single exposed sentence supplies both the site logic and the policy-and-team framing that separates the key from the three arm-site distractors.

testedDecision: Classify each Stage 3 finding as early improvement, ongoing unresolved risk, or not a primary superior vena cava response marker.
reason: This part grades response to treatment, and its own rows quote earlier values such as the prior neck circumference and the admission baseline, so the whole staged record is deliberately in scope. Stage 2 is the most plausible extra exposure, yet its worse readings are exactly the comparison data the classification demands rather than an unearned cue. No stage follows Stage 3, so nothing later can disclose these judgments.
